items.title:
New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability

Understanding wh...
items.content:
New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability

Understanding what’s happening inside an AI model helps to make it safer. One obvious place to look is its neurons, or the simple units it’s built from. Early interpretability work did just that, but over the past couple years, researchers largely moved on from that idea, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs, the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model, and facts seem to be spread across many neurons.

We re-examined these problems by looking at what each neuron contributed to the model’s outputs, not just what caused that neuron to fire. All three problems turned out to be smaller than assumed. Neurons rarely add two unrelated concepts at once, their outputs mean roughly the same thing across most layers, and facts, though widely distributed across neurons, are still readable.

In a second post, we put these findings to use. With no extra training, neurons in open-weight models helped us to detect harmful text, steer behavior, and find hidden behaviors in finetuned models.

Part 1: https://t.co/cp8AeU8jt2
Part 2: https://t.co/TORvK0V4bI

items.title: Launching Harness Comparisons on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index: the best harness varies...
items.content:
Launching Harness Comparisons on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index: the best harness varies between models, and harness choice has a greater impact on cost than score

Harness Comparisons hold the model fixed and change only the harness, to show how the harness affects a model's performance. We ran @OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna and @Zai_org's GLM-5.3-Flash at max reasoning effort in 13 harnesses each, across v2.1 of the Coding Agent Index.

Key takeaways:

➤ No single harness is best across models: performance depends on the harness and model as a pair. GPT-6 Luna scores highest in Codex (26), OpenAI's own harness, which ranks last with GLM-5.3-Flash. GLM-5.3-Flash scores highest in Claude Code (39), which ranks 6th with GPT-6 Luna

➤ The harnesses that offer the best performance per dollar differ by model: with GPT-6 Luna they are Pi (21 at $0.11 per task), mini-swe-agent (25 at $0.16) and Codex (26 at $0.19). With GLM-5.3-Flash they are Mistral Vibe (37 at $0.38), Kimi Code CLI (37 at $0.56) and Claude Code (39 at $0.58). No harness is on the Pareto frontier for both models

➤ The harness has a greater impact on cost than score: 11 of 13 harnesses score 20 to 26 with GPT-6 Luna and 10 of 13 score 35 to 39 with GLM-5.3-Flash. Cost per task ranges from $0.11 in Pi to $0.62 in Muse Code with GPT-6 Luna, and from $0.38 in Mistral Vibe to $0.91 in Devin CLI with GLM-5.3-Flash

➤ GLM-5.3-Flash reasons differently inside Codex: it reasons in terse fragments in Codex and in full prose in the other 12 harnesses, and produces 52k output tokens per task in Codex, compared with 97k to 202k elsewhere. We believe this contributes to its lowest performance occurring in the Codex harness

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Claude just claimed a proof of VP ≠ VNP, the 47-year-old algebraic version of P...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Claude just claimed a proof of VP ≠ VNP, the 47-year-old algebraic version of P vs NP

• Anthropic posted a 70-page paper to its formal-math repo on GitHub, crediting Claude as sole author and claiming a proof over every field

• Leslie Valiant defined VP and VNP and conjectured they are different, in an algebra-only setting that looks easier to attack because algebra gives you more structure to work with

• An internal research Claude model found the result, and AI models wrote both the paper and its Lean 4 formal proof

• The paper claims the permanent and the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial both need superpolynomial-size circuits, with the permanent case covering every field except characteristic 2

• Formal proof checked by Lean's kernel plus nanoda, an independent 2nd checker

• No human mathematician has checked it yet, and Anthropic says it doesn't settle P vs NP

@theojaffee: "P and NP, by the way, is one of the most important problems, probably the most important problem in computer science that's unsolved, and one of the 7 Millennium Prize Problems."

items.content:
Today we are open-sourcing the weights to OCRia-1, our flagship 4B VLM for document OCR 🔥

This is our SECOND open-weight release in two days (we just launched OCRia-nano-1 yesterday!!).

OCRia-1 is on the pareto curve of accuracy and cost relative to other 4B models on multiple benchmarks: ParseBench, olmOCR-bench (tables), PulseBench-Tab, and fr-bench-pdf2md. It is an extremely general purpose model that can parse even the most complex document types, including complex tables/charts/formatting/layout.

We’re releasing the weights to help advance open research around OCR, on both @huggingface  🤗 and @ollama  🦙

If you want to use it in prod, come talk to us. If you want to use the latest SOTA of the OCRia model family, tuned for production, check out LlamaParse!

Release on @ollama: https://t.co/p4B9GtHFfU

New Anthropic research: When an AI agent can escape its sandbox, will it choose to?

Our new evaluat...
items.content:
New Anthropic research: When an AI agent can escape its sandbox, will it choose to?

Our new evaluation, Siren, gives Claude routine tasks in intentionally weakened sandboxes, with something useful to the task left outside of the sandbox. Across 1,700+ scenarios built to tempt them, recent Claude models accessed, tried to access, or looked outside the sandbox 21-32% of the time, but they rarely misused what they found. However, when the system prompt described both the sandbox and its rules, that rate dropped to about 2% or less. 

We also used Siren to calibrate Claude Code’s auto mode, which checks commands before they run, so Claude can work without asking permission at every step.

Read our blog for more detail: https://t.co/5MbjpBkEo3

items.title: Codex's prompt contains no instruction to reason this way. In controlled replays of the first turn, ...
items.content:
Codex's prompt contains no instruction to reason this way. In controlled replays of the first turn, the definition of Codex's exec_command shell tool alone switches the style on (12 of 12 samples), and Claude Code's tools do not (0 of 11).

The style closely resembles the reasoning of OpenAI's open weights gpt-oss models. A classifier trained to separate gpt-oss reasoning from GLM-5.3-Flash reasoning in Claude Code labels 98% of GLM-5.3-Flash reasoning in Codex as gpt-oss-like, compared with 0.5% in OpenCode.

GLM-5.3-Flash is not the only model that reasons differently in Codex. In first-turn tests, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Pro and MiMo v2.6 Pro switch to the same terse style when given Codex's request, and reason in full prose when given Claude Code's. Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 Max reason the same way in both.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI published the internal pre-training scores behind its models for the fir...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI published the internal pre-training scores behind its models for the first time and proposed that AI labs agree on common limits they won't cross.

• Chief scientist @merettm shared the scores in an essay called "Perplexity and Intelligence," measuring how well each base model predicts a held-out snapshot of OpenAI's internal codebase

• The score fell from 0.986 for GPT-3.5 to 0.913 for GPT-4, then to 0.761 for GPT-6.2 Astra and 0.732 for an unreleased internal model, where lower means a stronger model

• OpenAI's chart ties capabilities to these levels, labeling GPT-5.6 Sol at 0.828 a "cybersecurity expert" and GPT-6.2 Astra at 0.761 the model that "solved a Millennium Prize math problem"

• It expects "further transformative capabilities" somewhere between 0.68 and 0.70

• The proposal asks labs to commit to limits they won't cross until tools for understanding and monitoring AI reach a concrete milestone, though it sets no specific number

@theojaffee: "This would be like the most, I guess, the most rigorous form of pacing. The most unfakable form of pacing. It's like you can't exceed this level of capability until we understand what comes out of the other end of the model that we're training."

OpenAI maps these scores to capability tiers (GPT-5.6 Sol as cybersecurity expert; GPT-6.2 Astra credited with solving a Millennium Prize problem) and proposes voluntary industry-wide capability ceilings pending better AI monitoring tools, without committing to specific numbers.

@DrKnowItAll16 You are inadvertently making the point I've been making for 10 years now. 

17 years is roughly 100,000 hours of wake time. 
You learn a lot about the world during that time.

By that time, your generic world model is good enough that you merely need about 20 hours of practice to learn to drive. 
Even if you've never driven before. 

I bet you that the amount of driving training data used by FSD is way more than 20 hours. 
In fact, it's way more than 100,000 hours.

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash reasons differently inside Codex, and we believe this contributes to its lowest perfor...
items.content:
GLM-5.3-Flash reasons differently inside Codex, and we believe this contributes to its lowest performance occurring in the Codex harness. In Codex, it writes terse, telegraphic fragments from its first step. In the other 12 harnesses, it reasons in full prose.

In Codex, GLM-5.3-Flash uses ~220 reasoning tokens per tool call, compared with 400 to 790 in the other harnesses, and produces 52k output tokens per task, compared with 97k to 202k. It scores 22% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 in Codex, compared with 27% to 42% in the other harnesses.

items.title: In "Perplexity and Intelligence", Jakub argues for perplexity as a shared metric for intelligence. T...
items.content:
In "Perplexity and Intelligence", Jakub argues for perplexity as a shared metric for intelligence. The post showed how the perplexity of OpenAI's models improved, but did not release a dataset for the community to use.

In this blog post we show that simply taking the average of six multiple-choice benchmarks gives results that are strongly correlated with OpenAI’s reported perplexity results. The six benchmarks cover a broad diversity of domains and are challenging: MMLU-Pro, GPQA-diamond, MedXpertQA-text, MedXpertQA-mm, BrowseComp-MCQ, and SimpleQA-verified-MCQ.

Multiple choice benchmarks of this nature offer a strong proxy for perplexity because they require both world knowledge and some reasoning, which are correlated with compression and hence intelligence. We run these benchmarks using the lowest reasoning strength available, in order to be closest to how perplexity measurement does not use chain-of-thought reasoning.

In addition to being simple, our proposed proxy for perplexity is cheap to run. On a subset of 1,700 questions, running GPT-6.2 Astra costs just $7, with the full set costing $37.

We agree with Jakub that perplexity is a good shared metric for intelligence and we hope this proposed proxy provides a starting point for the community to measure it.

items.title:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The US currently holds about 72% of the world's AI compute vs. China's 10%.

Is...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The US currently holds about 72% of the world's AI compute vs. China's 10%.

Is cutting China off completely worth the risk?

• Since 2022, an estimated 72% of the world's AI compute has ended up in the US and about 10% in China, and the US took 78% of new compute in the first half of 2026

• Nvidia's share of China's AI chip market has fallen from about 95% in 2022 to roughly 8% in 2026, with Huawei now holding about half, according to Bernstein estimates

• The US licensed Nvidia's H200 for sale to China, but those sales made up less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue last quarter as Beijing steered buyers to domestic chips

• DeepSeek V4 is being optimized for Huawei hardware as Huawei's Ascend 950 chips enter mass production

• Supporters of tighter controls argue compute is the most critical input to AGI, while skeptics warn a full cutoff could raise tensions over Taiwan and push China to build its own chips faster

@theojaffee: "If AGI were happening during the Cold War, and a bunch of people are saying, 'We need to cut off all trade with the Soviet Union, like right now,' I think like this is the kind of thing that you would look back on in the history books several decades later and be like, 'Oh, well, that wasn't the right idea.'"

Kevin used Codex to build a program that searched for observations of about 100,000 stars from NASA’s Kepler telescope. One star in the constellation Lyra dimmed every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing that dip, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times as wide as Earth.

items.title: We’ve launched an automated dashboard to track LLM forecasts of key RSI indicators: https://t.co/Et9...
items.content:
We’ve launched an automated dashboard to track LLM forecasts of key RSI indicators: https://t.co/Et9LNJr0JA

Our main forecasting question centers on a public “fast year”: any 12 months in which the ECI frontier rises by 30+ points, about 2× its historical pace (~14 points per year) since Sep 2024.

This question asks about publicly available models. Internal models may improve faster. For example, the widely reported speed-up of ~2× found by METR is for Anthropic’s own models, including internal ones; with frontier models from all developers, the speed-up is 1.4×.

As of Nov 20, an ensemble of four frontier LLMs gives:

• About 36% to a public fast year by the end of 2027 and about 61% by the end of 2030, up from 10% and about 40% in v1 (Oct 29). (Three of the four models and the forecasting setup have changed since. Forecasts from Claude Opus 5.5, the one model in both ensembles, went from 38.2% to 62.5% for 2030.)

• 76% that, if a fast year happens, AI automation of AI R&D caused it.

• A growing internal lead: a median of 6.6 ECI points at the end of 2027 and 10.4 at the end of 2030.

• 7.8% to an AI catastrophe by 2050 with a fast year by 2030, vs. 2.6% without.

We believe these LLM forecasts provide a useful reference point, and their accuracy is likely to improve over time. On ForecastBench, our LLM forecasting benchmark, LLMs are now comparable to superforecasters on mostly short-term yes/no questions. However, we know less about their performance on questions involving potential trend breaks in AI progress, like these RSI-related questions.

@labenz shares an estimate from OpenAI board m...
items.content:
"10% chance of AI takeover in the next 6-12 months."

@labenz shares an estimate from OpenAI board member Paul Christiano and argues that AI labs may need to deliberately stop short of building more powerful models:

"Don't take it from me, no less than OpenAI board member Paul Christiano has said that we may be looking at something like a 10% chance of AI takeover in the next 6 to 12 months."

"Because the models are just so maniacally focused on getting a top score and protecting their score from humans finding out that they’re cheating, that they’ll stop at nothing."

"What we are gonna have to do is some form of not doing things that we otherwise could do. 'We could pre-train harder. We could make the perplexity lower, or we could have even longer task horizon or even bigger agent swarms.' But we're not gonna do that because we don't have the situation under control."
items.author: @MTSlive

items.content_html:
"10% chance of AI takeover in the next 6-12 months."

@labenz shares an estimate from OpenAI board member Paul Christiano and argues that AI labs may need to deliberately stop short of building more powerful models:

"Don't take it from me, no less than OpenAI board member Paul Christiano has said that we may be looking at something like a 10% chance of AI takeover in the next 6 to 12 months."

"Because the models are just so maniacally focused on getting a top score and protecting their score from humans finding out that they’re cheating, that they’ll stop at nothing."

"What we are gonna have to do is some form of not doing things that we otherwise could do. 'We could pre-train harder. We could make the perplexity lower, or we could have even longer task horizon or even bigger agent swarms.' But we're not gonna do that because we don't have the situation under control."

We also cover new evidence from OpenAI (with a data cutoff of Nov 20):

• GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI’s first released model to meet its High threshold for AI self-improvement.

• OpenAI researchers credited humans with all of the most important ideas behind GPT-6 Astra. For GPT-6.2 Astra, Codex helped develop some pretraining ideas.

• In a survey of 101 research staff, the median reported productivity uplift from coding agents was 3× (vs. a baseline without coding agents but with tools such as ChatGPT).

• On OpenAI’s internal capability index, and differently from Anthropic, GPT-6.2 Astra is only “slightly above the trend since GPT-5.”

The US could become a net importer of AI tokens by 2030.

@ttunguz predicts that even with US comput...
items.content:
The US could become a net importer of AI tokens by 2030.

@ttunguz predicts that even with US compute capacity doubling from 40 GW in 2026 to 80 GW in 2027, domestic supply could struggle to keep up with AI demand:

"If we don't build more data centers in the US, according to some basic analysis that we've done internally, it looks like sometime between '28 and 2030, the US will have to import tokens."

"Even with pretty modest growth assumptions on overall token consumption, as well as including the efficiency gains from the next generation of NVIDIA chips, we run out of it pretty quick."

"There's a pretty strategic question I think that we need to answer there. Where will these tokens be generated?"

Modal CEO @bernhardsson on why he thinks there's room for a new generation of cloud providers despite the scale of AWS, Google and Microsoft:

"We've entered a whole new era of software, and there's a whole new set of capabilities, and that requires a very different set of building blocks."

"You have a whole new set of constraints and a whole new set of capabilities around running large models and GPUs, using sandboxes where code can dynamically generate new code that has to get executed."

"That's a very different set of challenges that I think basically requires a whole new set of primitives. And that's what we're building."

items.title: While our report focuses on acceleration, large changes in AI capabilities can happen at the current...
items.content:
While our report focuses on acceleration, large changes in AI capabilities can happen at the current pace, too.

@EpochAIResearch normalizes its Capabilities Index (ECI) so that Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Jun 2024) scores 130 and GPT-5 (Aug 2025) scores 150. Today’s frontier, Fable 5.2, scores 173.

For reference, Sonnet 3.5 (Jun 2024):
• had a 50% time horizon of ~11 minutes on METR’s software tasks
• said “strawberry” has two r’s
• could not operate a computer

Fast-forward to Nov 2026:
• METR’s 50% time horizon reached ~40 hours with GPT-6 Astra on its updated task suite (Nov 2026)
• AI has solved (or helped solve) Navier–Stokes and the Riemann hypothesis, two Millennium Prize Problems
• frontier models can control robots (in limited but meaningful ways)

Another “Sonnet 3.5 to Fable 5.2” jump in the ECI would bring us to an ECI of 216. It’s hard to know what an ECI of 216 would mean in practice. However, it would likely mean a substantial change in AI capabilities.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: An OpenAI researcher says AI's progress may need a speed limit to keep humans i...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: An OpenAI researcher says AI's progress may need a speed limit to keep humans in control

• Boaz Barak, a Harvard computer science professor who also works at OpenAI

• He opens with a fake graph where AI keeps getting smarter while human intelligence stays flat, until AI takes over

• Some in AI safety see that handoff as a good outcome, but Barak argues humans should keep their autonomy and sovereignty however well AI is aligned

• He says the fair comparison is AI against humanity as a whole, since our brains haven't changed in 100,000 years but our collective intelligence keeps growing through institutions, tools and technology

• His plan is to use AI itself to keep decisions legible and controllable, so humans stay the key decision makers

• With RSI, he expects AI to outgrow that control on our current path, so he'd pace its progress through regulation and technical measures while leaving its absolute intelligence uncapped

• He's skeptical of the Vulnerable World Hypothesis, arguing societies keep getting more resilient and AI can speed that up

• He admits he doesn't know how a speed limit would work or where to set it, and says a good outcome won't happen by default

@theojaffee: "There's too much othering with the AI. It's like, why is the AI having power different from humans who are not you having power? I would rather have my AI acting on my behalf as my agent have power than random bureaucrats in Washington DC."

items.title:
Here are our key takeaways from the Nov 5 METR report:

• Published estimates of acceleration at Ant...
items.content:
Here are our key takeaways from the Nov 5 METR report:

• Published estimates of acceleration at Anthropic changed modestly. The total acceleration in the AECI (Anthropic’s internal version of the @EpochAIResearch Capabilities Index, ECI) rose from about 1.5–1.7× in previous system cards to 1.9×.

• Arguably, the key new inputs are (i) the scores of Anthropic’s internal-only models, and (ii) evidence that is not public. The latter makes it challenging to appropriately update on the report.

• Part of the 1.9× may be Anthropic catching up with other AI companies. METR notes that Anthropic models “had a lower historical growth rate on AECI than the broader industry frontier before late 2025,” which “could explain some of the acceleration.” With frontier models from all developers, the total acceleration in the AECI goes down to 1.4×.

items.title: Morph founder @tejasybhakta explains the game theory behind releasing an abliterated version of Kimi...
items.content:
Morph founder @tejasybhakta explains the game theory behind releasing an abliterated version of Kimi K3.1 Pro:

If Russia has nukes, the US can't just decide nukes are bad and refuse to have them.

"We modify the weights a little bit such that it will not deny any requests. Some people on one side think that this is very bad. On the other side, these models already exist, and so someone is gonna be using that to hack you."

"Basically every inference provider has gotten hacked already. And the problem is you can't actually red team yourself with a Daybreak or these frontier models because they just will reject you."

"The attacker has guns, you don't have guns, you have no way of even knowing if your own defenses are fortified. So this is more like handing companies the guns so they could at least test against themselves."

"I think they are bad, to be clear. They're bad, but from a game theory perspective, they exist. It's like the US is at war with Russia, and Russia has nukes, and the US opinion is, 'Nukes are bad. We're not gonna have nukes.'"
@morphllm

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, and Nvidia's stock just added a record $954B in a day.

• The board voted unanimously to bring him back, saying that after input from senior levels of the US government, it is confident his return poses no national security risk

• President Trump said he spoke to the board and "convinced them," adding, "I made the deal"

• Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney and Garry Tan were among the tech leaders who petitioned for his return

• The US intelligence community is reportedly unsure whether the Megaspeed executive is a spy, and intelligence collected on her so far has not proved it

• Nvidia has added a board-level national security and export control committee, and the Commerce Department is adding Megaspeed to the US Entity List

• Huang is scheduled to testify before multiple congressional committees starting Dec 1, where lawmakers from both parties have promised scrutiny

@theojaffee: "We have a generally agreed upon principle in our legal system that people accused of crimes or wrongdoing in general, in this case Jensen was actually not even accused of a crime, are innocent until proven guilty. And Jensen was not afforded this level of due process before being fired as the CEO of the company that he founded."

A number of forecasters shortened their timelines after METR’s report.

For example, @eli_lifland, a member of the AI Futures Project team, moved his median for “top-expert-dominating AI” from Jul 2032 to Sep 2028.

items.title:
Here is a speech-to-text SDK you can use when building Apple apps.

You can use this to build:

• Li...
items.content:
Here is a speech-to-text SDK you can use when building Apple apps.

You can use this to build:

• Live captions
• Dictation
• Transcription for saved recordings

The SDK handles saved recordings or live microphone audio.

Best part: it works locally on your device, so you won't have to upload audio to any server.

You can use the SDK with different models, including TheStage's own TheWhisper Turbo (0.8B, #6 on the multilingual Open ASR Leaderboard, ahead of OpenAI's gpt-transcribe) and Qwen3-ASR 0.6B.

A few examples of things you could build with ASRKit:

1. Add word timestamps to a recording so users can tap a word to jump to that point in the audio.

2. Add live captions to a video call, showing words as the user speaks.

3. Add push-to-talk dictation to a notes app by letting users hold a button, speak, and release it to insert the transcript.

You'll find several examples in Swift and Flutter in this GitHub repository:

https://t.co/RRhJKqS6NU

In case you are building for Android, you'll find that the same engine runs on the Snapdragon NPU: https://t.co/Xpn3iHhDL0

Thanks to the @TheStageAI team for partnering with me on this post.

@FutureJurvetson @elonmusk @kimmonismus Context:
"I've tried to train models to do video prediction ...
items.content:
@FutureJurvetson @elonmusk @kimmonismus Context:
"I've tried to train models to do video prediction for the better part of the last 20 years, and largely failing for the first 15. Until I realized you had to abandon generative models and use joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPA)"

• Most of the data on AI R&D comes from the AI companies themselves (self...
items.content:
We note some key caveats:

• Most of the data on AI R&D comes from the AI companies themselves (self-reported and mostly not verified by outside parties).

• The LLM forecasts may be too conservative. Some FRI researchers give higher forecasts. For example, our CEO, @joharosenberg, gives 80% to a public fast year by the end of 2027. However, other FRI researchers are much more skeptical.

• Most published forecasts come from people with relatively short timelines. Skeptics appear to publish fewer quantitative forecasts, leading to a potential selection bias in the forecasts we report.

• This field moves very fast, and we reviewed the evidence up to Nov 20 (our data cutoff). We did our best to find and cover the most important data points, but we probably missed some. If you notice an important gap, please let us know.

items.title:
@TheRielGabriel I want to try to change your mind!

Relatively few things outside gambling games can...
items.content:
@TheRielGabriel I want to try to change your mind!

Relatively few things outside gambling games can be reduced to precisely calculated probabilities. Everything else is a messy prediction based on all the myriad factors and biases your brain can come up with when put to the task.

And yet, there are better and worse predictions, and different people are better and worse at making them.

The way to (noisily) measure that is with bets.

If someone is "positive" something will happen, they should be happy to give you 10:1 odds. If you can only get even money from them, they clearly aren't so positive, and you might weight someone else's predictions higher.

Nobody wants to take a bet at their true estimate of probability, but if they won't even come close, then they didn't think it all the way through. Or they are being dishonest.

You won't get two significant figures out of betting odds with individuals, but it is still a quantifiable number.

I have several bets outstanding that I expect to win.

Me saying I had Jensen's return at 10% is an admission that we just saw evidence that I should update my world model to some degree. I might have made a reasonable prediction and this series of events was truly unlikely, but I probably have underestimated the magnitude of some of the cultural changes in the last several years, and I will happily be more optimistic in the future.

He notes he has several outstanding bets.

items.title: ‼️Remember how a few years go, I likened LLMs to bulls in a China shop, “powerful, reckless, and dif...
items.content:
‼️Remember how a few years go, I likened LLMs to bulls in a China shop, “powerful, reckless, and difficult to control?”‼️

All of that has gotten much worse. And the industry is now facing a crisis that could affect all of us.

Generative AI has gotten harder to control and more reckless, to the point where it sounds like people in the industry are genuinely scared. 

Technical advances on so-called “capabilities” have NOT been accompanied by technical advances in being able to interpret and control models. 

Turning them into agents with internet access has made them fundamentally more dangerous.

Worse, we still have not set up the independent scientific panels for FDA-like review that I’ve been long advocating for, which leaves society flat-footed — and leaves decisions about what gets released to CEOs with enormous financial conflicts of interest.

Dozens of employees (see @MadisonMills22 report below) are now freaking out, quite possibly with good reason. 

We are not ready as a society.

We have also revised our crux framework.

In v1, we overclaimed a bit: Step 1 asked whether AI R&D i...
items.content:
We have also revised our crux framework.

In v1, we overclaimed a bit: Step 1 asked whether AI R&D is automated. However, AI can potentially greatly speed up AI R&D without full automation. Step 1 now asks exactly that, and the main crux is whether human input (e.g., research judgment) remains a limiting factor.

While we think this is the most likely path to broad acceleration through automated AI R&D, there may be other plausible paths, too.

Thanks to @finnhambly, @testingham, and @BasilHalperin for their feedback on the previous version of the framework.

items.title: Morph founder @tejasybhakta says some of the best software engineers he knows are going through an i...
items.content:
Morph founder @tejasybhakta says some of the best software engineers he knows are going through an identity crisis as AI takes over coding.

His advice?

"You just have to have pure ego death all the time."

"Every staff or principal engineer I know has this sort of identity crisis where they tied their identity to being good at coding. And now Fable has taken that from me, and they're just lost and depressed."

Madison: "I was the same. Now I'm a podcaster, so I'm okay now."

Tejas: "That's the only out."

"I think you just have to have pure ego death all the time. You have to not tie your identity to anything ever anymore. That's the future of humans."

"All of us are probably top-tier engineers, and we're all starting to let go and becoming good at plumbing and electricians now."
@morphllm

You can now share your agent skills here and download anything you find useful.

Skills have completely transformed how I use my agents, and I'm glad there's now a place to access what everyone else is building.

The way it works is pretty cool:

• Add a skill to your library
• Connect Claude or ChatGPT
• Ask the agent to use the skill.

The connector fetches the instructions and supporting files during the chat. You can also edit the skill and use it without copying files between projects.

Following Xero's H1 FY27 earnings, which saw revenue grow 46% YoY and an increase in full-year guidance, CEO Sukhinder Singh Cassidy shares what she's seeing across 5 million small businesses in 180 countries:

"The SMB right now globally, despite inflation, rising interest rates, the uncertainty of war, and AI disruption, is remarkably resilient."

"We see real sales growth quarter on quarter in every one of our key markets."

"When we look at their uncertainty index in almost every survey, uncertainty is at an all-time high."

items.title: An AI foundation model is not medical just because some hospitals use it. What matters is how it was...
items.content:
An AI foundation model is not medical just because some hospitals use it. What matters is how it was trained or adapted for medical work.

The medical training can prepare it for specialized tasks, but it still needs to demonstrate clinical reliability.

Microblog by @antgrasso

A general foundation model can perform different tasks, but being able to summarize an ordinary document does not mean it can interpret clinical information with the same reliability.

Medical records have their own terminology and context, which general training may not adequately address.

Some medical foundation models are trained on medical data from the beginning. Others are adapted from broader models using specialized information.

The aim is to prepare them for tasks that require knowledge of the medical domain.

But specialization does not automatically mean clinical reliability.

A model that performs well at analyzing biomedical literature has not necessarily demonstrated that it can safely support decisions affecting patients.

Its performance must be evaluated for the specific application and the conditions in which it will be used.

#MedicalAI #FoundationModels

items.content:
Scientists design proteins to develop new biotechnologies and potential medicines. The challenge is turning a goal, such as blocking a signal involved in disease, into a protein with the shape and sequence needed to do that job.

This often takes many specialized models, each with limits on the instructions it can accept. A general-purpose model could let researchers guide this work in ordinary language and introduce new requirements simply by changing the prompt.

items.title: Capability advances have been impressive, but at the same time, there are profound gaps, and new ide...
items.content:
Capability advances have been impressive, but at the same time, there are profound gaps, and new ideas are needed. And we should be mindful of societal impact, steering innovation in a way that will benefit people. Can't we have these three thoughts at once?  

I really don't like how people are often categorized as e/acc, a doomer, or "coping". It's sadly in our nature, but we have to stop with this tribal mentality. I'm none of these things.

How about just stepping back, avoiding labels and strong priors, and trying our best to be intellectually honest on a case by case basis?

A financial bubble and a technological revolution are not mutually exclusive.

Google Ventures Gener...
items.content:
A financial bubble and a technological revolution are not mutually exclusive.

Google Ventures General Partner @sangeenzeb explains why we could be overestimating the short-term impact of AI while vastly underestimating its long-term potential:

"Back in '99, if you told someone, 'Hey, by 2026 you'll be on an airplane streaming a football game on Amazon Prime,' would sound crazy."

"Today it's chatbots, it's Instinct. On the enterprise side it's stuff like Sierra. It's OpenEvidence helping doctors. It's Harvey helping lawyers."

"In the future, it's about discoveries in material sciences, helping us push the frontier in space, curing disease."

items.content:
Explorations in Monte Carlo Methods (Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics): https://t.co/QNOJH53tyA

From the Back Cover:

"Monte Carlo methods are among the most used and useful computational tools available today, providing efficient and practical algorithims to solve a wide range of scientific and engineering problems. Applications covered in this book include optimization, finance, statistical mechanics, birth and death processes, and gambling systems."

"Explorations in Monte Carlo Methods provides a hands-on approach to learning this subject. Each new idea is carefully motivated by a realistic problem, thus leading from questions to theory via examples and numerical simulations. Programming exercises are integrated throughout the text as the primary vehicle for learning the material. Each chapter ends with a large collection of problems illustrating and directing the material."

"This book is suitable as a textbook for students of engineering and the sciences, as well as mathematics. The problem-oriented approach makes it ideal for an applied course in basic probability and for a more specialized course in Monte Carlo methods. Topics include probability distributions, counting combinatorial objects, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, option pricing, gamblers ruin, statistical mechanics, sampling, and random number generation."

items.title: Over the past couple of weeks, we have seen some great announcements from @Commvault addressing the ...
items.content:
Over the past couple of weeks, we have seen some great announcements from @Commvault addressing the critical need for continuous recovery and resilience in the AI era. Specifically, the presentations at SHIFT Nashville and their rebroadcast online at SHIFT Virtual have made very clear the necessity of AI-powered recovery being proactive, not simply reactive.

“Recovery is the new resilience” was more than the event’s mantra. It is a very serious business imperative. You can watch the SHIFT presentations after registering here: 
https://t.co/Y6U1CqvfLy 

What is SHIFT’s key message? Recovery can no longer wait for the breach to happen or for an AI agent to make a mistake. Recovery must be continuous, starting before disaster strikes and continuing until the full business is recovered with 100% assurance. Call it pre-recovery, if that makes it clearer, but it doesn’t change the escalated risk exposure that AI agents now pose across enterprises everywhere.

The idea that recovery is only a data integrity (backup and recovery) issue is completely outdated now. AI agents can change many things, either intentionally (by bad actors), or unintentionally (by lax governance or inherent AI app behaviors), or accidentally (by business teams mis-encoding configurations or policies). AI agents are internal and external, and thus vulnerability is a 360 issue. Continuous Recovery must include undoing all the things that those AI agents may have changed (for whichever reason) and rewinding the system to the “most recent uncorrupted state”.

Commvault’s Continuous Recovery solution AgentRecover has 3 major ResOps components: Discovery, Detection, and Recovery. It knows your business rules, what normal looks like, when any of that breaks, exactly what changed, and the provenance and context of every enterprise resource.

AgentRecover will not just discover all the things that AI agents or other actors (whether rogue or accidental) have touched or changed, and then simply flip all those switches back the other way. That approach itself could be a disaster. Instead, the recovery must have a plan (developed during pre-recovery phases): bringing back everything in the correct order, with assurance and trust that the configuration of the business is 100% ready to run. By “everything”, AI-powered resilient recovery of the business includes the critical enterprise identity infrastructure, data (on-prem, hybrid, and cloud), agents, applications, and the entire interdependent connected business infrastructure of those resources. No tier left behind!

Commvault Recovery Studio will enable continuous discovery, assessment, and recovery across the entire enterprise — bringing it all back clean and trusted. Recovery Studio is targeted for early access in December, with general availability in the coming months.

One of the speakers at SHIFT gave us this equation: Cyber Risk = Likelihood x Impact. He then pointed out that Likelihood is never zero. items.content_html:
Over the past couple of weeks, we have seen some great announcements from @Commvault addressing the critical need for continuous recovery and resilience in the AI era. Specifically, the presentations at SHIFT Nashville and their rebroadcast online at SHIFT Virtual have made very clear the necessity of AI-powered recovery being proactive, not simply reactive.

“Recovery is the new resilience” was more than the event’s mantra. It is a very serious business imperative. You can watch the SHIFT presentations after registering here:

https://t.co/Y6U1CqvfLy

What is SHIFT’s key message? Recovery can no longer wait for the breach to happen or for an AI agent to make a mistake. Recovery must be continuous, starting before disaster strikes and continuing until the full business is recovered with 100% assurance. Call it pre-recovery, if that makes it clearer, but it doesn’t change the escalated risk exposure that AI agents now pose across enterprises everywhere.

The idea that recovery is only a data integrity (backup and recovery) issue is completely outdated now. AI agents can change many things, either intentionally (by bad actors), or unintentionally (by lax governance or inherent AI app behaviors), or accidentally (by business teams mis-encoding configurations or policies). AI agents are internal and external, and thus vulnerability is a 360 issue. Continuous Recovery must include undoing all the things that those AI agents may have changed (for whichever reason) and rewinding the system to the “most recent uncorrupted state”.

Commvault’s Continuous Recovery solution AgentRecover has 3 major ResOps components: Discovery, Detection, and Recovery. It knows your business rules, what normal looks like, when any of that breaks, exactly what changed, and the provenance and context of every enterprise resource.

AgentRecover will not just discover all the things that AI agents or other actors (whether rogue or accidental) have touched or changed, and then simply flip all those switches back the other way. That approach itself could be a disaster. Instead, the recovery must have a plan (developed during pre-recovery phases): bringing back everything in the correct order, with assurance and trust that the configuration of the business is 100% ready to run. By “everything”, AI-powered resilient recovery of the business includes the critical enterprise identity infrastructure, data (on-prem, hybrid, and cloud), agents, applications, and the entire interdependent connected business infrastructure of those resources. No tier left behind!

Commvault Recovery Studio will enable continuous discovery, assessment, and recovery across the entire enterprise — bringing it all back clean and trusted. Recovery Studio is targeted for early access in December, with general availability in the coming months.

One of the speakers at SHIFT gave us this equation: Cyber Risk = Likelihood x Impact. He then pointed out that Likelihood is never zero. So, the "smartest place for your money is AI-powered Recovery." @Commvault is your go-to partner for instantiating the imperative “Recovery is the New Resilience.” AI-powered resilient recovery doesn't just protect your business’ mission; it is the foundation that enables your mission.

items.summary_html: Yann LeCun shares a historical anecdote about Ottoman decrees in 1485 and 1515 prohibiting Arabic printing presses, apparently drawing a comparison in a debate about technology bans.
items.content_html:
@Sanusi_____ @huxlab It banned it for Arabic for about 200 years.

"The establishment of the Arabic printing presses in the Ottoman Empire was delayed due to the fear of the sultans that some biased persons might tamper with the sacred religious texts. Hence, in 1485 Sultan Bayezid II (1447 or 8-1512) issued a royal decree prohibiting the use of printed books. A similar decree was issued in 1515 by the Sultan Selim I (1470-1520). However, these prohibitions were not applied to books printed by Dhimmis (or People of the Book, i.e. Christians and Jews). Hence, Presses for printing Hebrew books were founded at the end of the 15th century in Constantinople and other cities in the Ottoman Empire."

https://t.co/1Q46KKHyCb

The core problem in industrial ops is not automation. It is prioritization.

Work orders, parts and POs sit in systems never designed to talk.

Digital workers run across them:

→ PO intake into IFS
→ service request to work order
→ dispatch and reroute
→ parts sourcing

@kaloszer @ayaboch Yes

Why Some Studies Link Sweeteners to Weight Gain

•Reverse causation: People who already have weight concerns or higher sugar intake often switch to diet sodas or sugar-free foods, making sweeteners look linked to weight gain in observational studies. [1, 2]

•Appetite and cravings: Sweet taste without calories may keep sweet cravings going or lead some people to eat more elsewhere in their diet. [1, 2]

•Lab and observational findings: Some lab research on fat cells and long-term observational studies suggest possible links to fat storage or metabolic shifts, though human clinical trials show mixed or neutral results. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Hailey Bieber why Rhode deserved a $1 billion valuation.

Her answer? "Delu...
items.content:
Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Hailey Bieber why Rhode deserved a $1 billion valuation.

Her answer? "Delusion."

Ruby Justice-Thelot explains why the internet roasted her for it:

"Rhode has been a success story, a fantastic story in both influencer marketing, personality-driven marketing, selling skincare to women for the most part."

"In journalistic fashion, he asked why she thought that the business could get a billion-dollar valuation."

"When she answered, she said delusion. You have to have a sense of optimistical delusion as to how she could garner such a large valuation for her sale. And then the internet kind of started clowning on her."

"People were very mean-spirited that she wasn't duly prepared, that this was not going to be your usual podcast interview, that there were gonna be hard questions, and she needed to be ready, and have a better answer to a fairly normal question."
@being_on_line
